questions.content: After applying a 3×3 box filter (mean filter) to an image, the image will become:
questions.analysis: A mean filter replaces each pixel with the average of its neighborhood, which is equivalent to low-pass filtering. High-frequency details (edges, noise) are attenuated because they represent the largest local variations. The result is a smoother, more blurred image.

options.content: Blurrier (smoothed)
Sharper
Brighter
Higher contrast

questions.content: The correct sequence of steps in the Canny edge detection algorithm is:
questions.analysis: The standard Canny pipeline is: ① Gaussian smoothing for noise reduction; ② Compute gradient magnitude and direction (typically with Sobel operators); ③ Non-maximum suppression to thin edges; ④ Double thresholding + hysteresis to determine final edges. Non-maximum suppression must precede double thresholding; otherwise, thick edges would remain.

options.content: Gaussian smooth → gradient computation → non-maximum suppression → double threshold + hysteresis
Gradient computation → Gaussian smooth → double threshold + hysteresis → non-maximum suppression
Gaussian smooth → double threshold + hysteresis → gradient computation → non-maximum suppression
Non-maximum suppression → Gaussian smooth → gradient computation → double threshold + hysteresis

questions.content: The SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) descriptor is invariant to which of the following transformations?
questions.analysis: SIFT's core design goals are scale invariance (achieved via the DoG pyramid) and rotation invariance (achieved via dominant orientation assignment). It also exhibits partial robustness to affine transformations, illumination changes, and viewpoint changes, but not full invariance. SIFT is not translation-invariant in a strict sense — keypoint locations shift with the image — but the descriptor is computed relative to the local patch, so detection and matching are robust to translation.

options.content: Scale and rotation
Arbitrary affine transformations
Arbitrary perspective transformations
Translation

questions.content: The Harris corner detector uses the eigenvalues λ₁ and λ₂ of the structure tensor (second-moment matrix) M to classify points. When a pixel is classified as a corner:
questions.analysis: The core idea of Harris corner detection: at a corner, shifting a window in any direction produces a large intensity change. The eigenvalues λ₁ and λ₂ of the structure tensor M represent the magnitude of intensity change along the two principal directions. At a corner, both directions exhibit large change → both λ₁ and λ₂ are large. At an edge, only one direction has large change → λ₁ ≫ λ₂ or vice versa. In a flat region, both are small.

options.content: Both λ₁ and λ₂ are large
λ₁ is large, λ₂ is small
Both λ₁ and λ₂ are small
λ₁ ≈ −λ₂

questions.content: In the pinhole camera model, which of the following belongs to the intrinsic parameters?
questions.analysis: Intrinsic parameters describe the camera's own geometric and optical properties, including focal length (f_x, f_y), principal point (c_x, c_y), and distortion coefficients. Extrinsic parameters describe the camera's pose in the world coordinate frame, including the rotation matrix R and translation vector t. Focal length and principal point are elements of the intrinsic matrix K.

options.content: Focal length f and principal point (c_x, c_y)
Rotation matrix R
Translation vector t
World coordinate system origin

question_groups.title: The Role of CNN Pooling Layers

questions.content: Which of the following is NOT a primary function of pooling layers in CNNs?
questions.analysis: Pooling layers serve three main purposes: ① downsampling (reducing spatial dimensions and computation); ② providing translation invariance; ③ expanding the receptive field of subsequent layers. Pooling does NOT increase the number of channels — channel count is determined by the number of filters in convolutional layers. In fact, pooling preserves the channel count unchanged.

options.content: Increasing the number of feature map channels
Reducing the spatial resolution of feature maps
Providing a degree of translation invariance
Expanding the receptive field of subsequent convolutional layers

questions.content: The Lucas-Kanade optical flow method is based on which core assumption?
questions.analysis: Lucas-Kanade optical flow relies on three assumptions: ① brightness constancy — the intensity of a pixel remains unchanged after motion; ② small motion — motion between adjacent frames is small enough for a first-order Taylor approximation; ③ spatial coherence — neighboring pixels share the same motion. Among these, brightness constancy is the fundamental premise of the optical flow constraint equation.

options.content: Brightness constancy
Color constancy
Objects must be rigid bodies
The scene must be static

questions.content: The Hough Transform is most commonly used in computer vision for:
questions.analysis: The core idea of the Hough Transform is to map geometric shapes from image space to parameter space and use a voting mechanism. Its most classic application is detecting straight lines (using polar parameters ρ, θ) in edge maps, but it can also be extended to detect circles, ellipses, and other parametric shapes. It does not perform smoothing, segmentation, or classification.

options.content: Detecting geometric shapes such as lines and circles
Smoothing and denoising images
Segmenting different texture regions
Classifying images

questions.content: Regarding the difference between semantic segmentation and instance segmentation, which statement is correct?
questions.analysis: Semantic segmentation assigns a class label (e.g., 'person', 'car') to every pixel but does not distinguish between different individuals of the same class — all people in an image receive the same 'person' label. Instance segmentation goes further: it not only knows which pixels belong to 'person' but also distinguishes 'person #1' from 'person #2'. Mask R-CNN is a representative model for instance segmentation.

options.content: Semantic segmentation does not distinguish individuals within a class; instance segmentation does
Semantic segmentation is finer-grained than instance segmentation and can distinguish each object instance
The two are identical; only the name differs
Instance segmentation can only detect a single object; semantic segmentation can detect multiple objects

questions.content: In object detection, the standard IoU (Intersection over Union) threshold is typically 0.5. A predicted box with IoU > 0.5 against a ground-truth box is considered a True Positive. When the threshold is raised from 0.5 to 0.75:
questions.analysis: The IoU threshold determines how strict the matching criterion is. Raising the threshold from 0.5 to 0.75 means the predicted box must overlap more with the ground-truth box to count as correct — a stricter standard. This reduces TP (some predictions that barely met the 0.5 threshold now fail), while increasing FN (they become missed detections) and FP (they fail to match any ground-truth and count as false alarms). As a result, mAP typically drops.

options.content: mAP typically decreases because the matching criterion is stricter
mAP typically increases because low-quality matches are removed
mAP stays the same; the IoU threshold does not affect the final result
It depends on the specific dataset and cannot be determined
